This guy has great videos. That said, he's smart enough to know this doesn't work for all stiffs who know that time is money.

Wrapping a cord in a tight loop like he showed is a rookie mistake. And hook-looping a cord has a place for sure, and I use that for heavy cords. But for powering a device like a vacuum pump, which is often used on a rooftop, which always has limited outlets, a Jesus wrap is the way to go.

Rather than looping it around an arm, you use your arm spread for making the loops. You start with the female end in one hand, do a full arms stretch to grab the cord on-the-run (back towards your source of dancing pixies), and repeat. You don't twist or rotate your hands while doing this, and you get no twist in the cord. Your cord developes memory that makes it easier over time.

The biggest advantage to this method is how it gets extended. With cord wrapped from storage, you stand next to the power source, hold the male end and throw the package towards your work area. Then you can easily gauge what length cord you will need to add to reach your work area, or if you have enough.

The second advantage is that you don't have to walk the male end back to the outlet, it's already connected before you go to the female end.

The third advantage is a compact bundle that can easily be hung on your cord hook in your work van, instead of a big (untangled) heap on the floor.

Oh, and when tying extensions together, or the tool to the cord, don't grab each cord and make a simple knot, that shit comes apart when you are say, using a power tool on a ladder for instance. Instead, connect cords together, grab the cords with one hand about a foot down from the connection, then make a simple knot. So instead of just a singular cord being on each side of the knot, you have double cords on one side, and the connection junction on the other.
